clinicalPearls: The commonest autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, defined by primary adrenal insufficiency with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes
It is more common in adults and in women, with a polygenic and HLA-associated inheritance rather than a single gene
The combination of Addison disease and autoimmune thyroid disease is known as Schmidt syndrome
Other associated autoimmune conditions include coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and premature ovarian insufficiency
Starting thyroid hormone before treating coexisting adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis
Screening at-risk individuals and relatives for evolving endocrine autoimmunity is important
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is a polygenic disorder of immune tolerance, strongly associated with particular HLA haplotypes and other susceptibility genes, in which organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells target several endocrine glands. Unlike type 1, there is no single causative gene. Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex, thyroid and pancreatic beta cells produces the characteristic cluster, and the tempo of gland involvement varies, with components often appearing years apart.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of adrenal, thyroid and glucose status
Screening for coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia
HLA and family assessment where appropriate
redFlags: Adrenal crisis, especially if thyroid hormone is started first
Unexplained hypoglycaemia or reduced insulin requirement signalling adrenal insufficiency
reference.prognosis: With appropriate hormone replacement and monitoring the prognosis is good, but unrecognised adrenal insufficiency, particularly during intercurrent illness or after starting thyroxine, can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Giving thyroid hormone before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency
Attributing improving diabetes control to good management when it reflects Addison disease
Missing associated coeliac disease or pernicious anaemia
Failing to monitor for evolving components
management: Hormone replacement for each affected gland: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid for Addison's disease, levothyroxine for autoimmune thyroid disease and insulin for type 1 diabetes
Commence adrenal glucocorticoid replacement before starting levothyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis
Adrenal crisis prevention through sick-day glucocorticoid dosing, emergency parenteral hydrocortisone and patient education with alert identification
Screen for and manage associated coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and premature ovarian insufficiency
Lifelong surveillance for evolving endocrine autoimmunity using organ-specific autoantibodies and biochemistry
Screen at-risk relatives for endocrine autoimmunity
